opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
When I first read this Gospel years ago, I struggled with it. Jesus says He was sent “only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,” and then compares a Gentile woman to the household dogs waiting for scraps from the table. At first, those words made me feel like God had favorites—that unless you were born into Israel, you somehow didn’t fully belong.

Over time, I began to understand that this was never the point.

Jesus came to fulfill God’s covenant with Israel. God had chosen Israel not because they were greater than other nations, but because through them He would reveal Himself to the world and ultimately bring forth the Messiah. God’s promise always had the whole world in view. Israel was the beginning of the story, not the end of it.

The Canaanite woman beautifully demonstrates this truth. She could have been offended. She could have walked away believing she had been rejected. Instead, she remained steadfast in faith. She trusted that even a crumb of God’s mercy would be enough. Jesus then publicly praises her faith and heals her daughter, revealing that God’s mercy is not limited by ancestry, nationality, or status. Faith is the doorway into His kingdom.

This Gospel reminds us that God’s plan unfolded in stages, just as He had promised throughout salvation history. Jesus first fulfilled the covenant with Israel, then, through His death and resurrection, opened that covenant to every nation. What seems at first to be a story of exclusion becomes one of the clearest demonstrations that no one is beyond the reach of God’s grace.

Perhaps that is why Jesus allowed this encounter to unfold as it did. He wasn’t teaching us who was unworthy; He was showing us that genuine faith overcomes every barrier we think separates us from God. The woman did not let offense become an obstacle to grace. She trusted, persevered, and received far more than she dared to ask.

That is the invitation for all of us. We may approach Christ feeling unworthy, forgotten, or outside the circle. But if we come to Him with humble, persistent faith, we discover what this woman discovered: there is a place for us at His table.
